q2.answer: In the bone of the gums (upper jaw), next to the front teeth. It is called the alveolar cleft.

q3.answer: The lateral incisor, the small tooth next to the front tooth, never grew (agenesis). About half of children with a cleft do not have it on the cleft side.

q4.answer: The eye tooth needs bone to grow into and come down through. The graft gives it that bone.
q4.where: Sheet 1, 'The eye tooth' and 'Why surgeons do the bone graft'

q5.answer: About 8 to 11 years old. The team picks the time by how far the teeth have grown, not by age. The best time is before the eye tooth comes through.

q6.answer: Most often from the hip. It is soft, spongy bone.

q7.answer: New bone fills the gap and the gum has healed over it. It joins the two parts of the upper jaw. The eye tooth is a little lower but still in the bone.
q7.where: Sheet 2, key message box and 'What has changed'

q8.answer: With an X-ray at about 3 to 6 months after surgery. It shows how well the new bone has taken.

q9.answer: The hip can be sore for a while after the bone is taken. In one study, children went back to school about 2 weeks after surgery.

q10.answer: It has come down through the new bone and is fully in the row of teeth.
q10.where: Sheet 3, key message box and 'What has changed'

q11.answer: Fixed braces. Almost everyone who has this graft needs them.

q12.answer: Two main plans. 1) Close the space: braces move the eye tooth into the missing tooth's place, and the dentist reshapes it and adds tooth-coloured filling. This is the most common plan for children with a cleft. 2) Keep the space: while still growing, a removable plate holds a false tooth. After growth stops, the dentist can fill the gap for good with an implant (post in the bone with a crown) or a bridge (false tooth with one wing glued to the back of the next tooth). The cleft team will talk it through with you.
